name: Kyanjin Gompa
tagline: Monastery village at 3,870 m below Langtang Lirung and Kyanjin Ri
meta_description: Kyanjin Gompa (3,870 m) is the high point of the Langtang Valley trek: Kyanjin Ri at 4,773 m, a 1955 yak cheese factory and glacier walks. Plan your days.
summary: Kyanjin Gompa is the last permanent settlement in the Langtang Valley, a cluster of lodges around a small monastery at 3,870 m, reached in three walking days from Syabrubesi. Most trekkers stay two nights to climb Kyanjin Ri (4,773 m), taste yak cheese and look straight up at Langtang Lirung (7,227 m).
intro: The Langtang Valley opens out at Kyanjin Gompa into a wide glacial basin ringed by peaks. Langtang Lirung, 7,227 m, rises to the north with its hanging glaciers, Kyanjin Ri and Tserko Ri stand behind the lodges, and the valley carries on east past Langshisa towards the Tibetan border. The village takes its name from the gompa, a small Tibetan Buddhist monastery on a rise above the lodges, which was damaged in 2015 and has since been repaired.

For most trekkers Kyanjin is the turning point. It sits at 3,870 m, high enough that a rest day is wise, and the classic plan is to arrive around midday, visit the monastery and the yak cheese factory, then climb Kyanjin Ri early the next morning before heading back down. Strong walkers add Tserko Ri at 4,984 m, a longer and harder hike, or walk up the valley to Langshisa Kharka at about 4,100 m for glacier views.

Kyanjin's lodges were rebuilt and enlarged after the earthquake and are now among the more comfortable teahouses in the region, with solar power, dining rooms warmed by stoves and some rooms with attached bathrooms. Yaks graze the flats around the airstrip-like meadow, and the Swiss-founded cheese factory, started in 1955, still sells its hard yak cheese by the slice. Nights are cold: expect −5 to −10 °C in December and January, and frost even in October.
facts: Kathmandu, plus a helicopter landing area at Kyanjin
≈ 122 km drive to Syabrubesi + 3 days' walk, or ≈ 40 min by helicopter
Kyanjin Ri, yak cheese factory, Langtang Lirung views

highlights.title: Kyanjin Ri sunrise climb
highlights.text: Kyanjin Ri rises about 900 m above the village. The main summit is 4,773 m and a lower prayer-flag top sits a little below it. From the top you see Langtang Lirung, Gangchenpo, Naya Kanga and the glaciers feeding the valley. Allow 3–4 hours up and 2 down.

highlights.title: Yak cheese factory
highlights.text: Founded with Swiss help in 1955, the Kyanjin cheese factory buys milk from herders in the upper valley and makes a firm yellow cheese. You can buy it by weight, eat it on toast in the lodges and see the simple wooden presses in the season when it is working.

highlights.title: Kyanjin Gompa monastery
highlights.text: The small monastery on the knoll above the lodges is the spiritual centre of the upper valley. Butter lamps, prayer wheels and a view down the valley reward the five-minute climb. Visit in the late afternoon when it is quiet and the light falls on Langtang Lirung.

highlights.title: Tserko Ri for strong walkers
highlights.text: Tserko Ri, at 4,984 m, is a long day of 8–9 hours with about 1,100 m of ascent on loose trail. It gives a wider panorama than Kyanjin Ri, including Yala Peak and the peaks along the Tibetan border, but should only be attempted after a night at Kyanjin and with good weather.

highlights.title: Langshisa Kharka and the upper valley
highlights.text: An easier full-day walk heads east along the valley floor past yak pastures to Langshisa Kharka at about 4,100 m. The route gains little height, passes moraines and gives close views of the Langshisa Ri peaks and the snout of the Langtang Glacier.

highlights.title: Helicopter breakfast landing
highlights.text: Helicopter tours from Kathmandu land at Kyanjin in about 40 minutes for a short stop with breakfast and views of Langtang Lirung. It is the fastest way to see the upper valley, though weather and the 3,870 m altitude mean it is not for everyone.

how_to_reach.text: From Syabrubesi, walk three days up the Langtang Khola: about 6 hours to Lama Hotel, 6–7 hours to Langtang village and 3–4 hours to Kyanjin Gompa. The climb is steady, from 1,460 m to 3,870 m, with no passes to cross.
No road reaches Kyanjin. The nearest road-head is Syabrubesi, about 122 km and 7–8 hours by bus or jeep from Kathmandu via Trishuli Bazaar and Dhunche.

Charter and shared helicopter tours fly from Kathmandu to Kyanjin in about 40 minutes and land on the meadow near the village, weather permitting. Flights go in the early morning, before clouds build up in the valley around midday.

where_to_stay: Kyanjin has around two dozen teahouse lodges grouped on the flat ground below the monastery, all rebuilt or enlarged since 2015. Expect twin rooms with foam mattresses and blankets, solar or gas showers for a fee, charging for a fee and dining rooms with a central stove. A few newer lodges have attached bathrooms and double-glazed windows; book ahead in October and April when groups fill them. There are no star-rated hotels. We pick lodges near the cheese factory end of the village for shorter walks to the Kyanjin Ri trail. Bring a four-season sleeping bag, because rooms are unheated and nights drop well below zero from November to March.
tips: Arrive by early afternoon so you can walk to the monastery and cheese factory before the wind picks up.
Start Kyanjin Ri by 5:30 am in spring and autumn to beat the cloud that often fills the valley by 10 am.
Do not go higher than Kyanjin on arrival day if you have a headache; rest, drink water and tell your guide.
Buy a block of yak cheese at the end of your stay, not on arrival, so you are not carrying it up and down the hills.
Charging and hot showers cost extra, so carry a power bank and small notes in rupees.

experiences.title: Kyanjin Ri sunrise hike to 4,773 m
experiences.image_query: Kyanjin Ri summit prayer flags Langtang Lirung
experiences.summary: The classic acclimatisation and viewpoint climb from Kyanjin Gompa, gaining about 900 m on a steep grassy and rocky trail to prayer flags at 4,773 m. On a clear morning it gives the widest view in the Langtang Valley.
body: Kyanjin Ri is the hill directly behind the village, and the climb starts within ten minutes of your lodge. Most groups leave between 5 and 6 am with headlamps, zigzagging up yak pastures and then a rockier ridge. There are two tops: a lower one with prayer flags at roughly 4,600 m, which many trekkers treat as their summit, and the true top at 4,773 m about 30–45 minutes further along the ridge.

From the top the panorama is close and big. Langtang Lirung, 7,227 m, fills the view to the west with its icefalls, while Kimshung, Gangchenpo, Naya Kanga and the peaks on the Tibetan border ring the valley. Below you the lodges of Kyanjin look tiny beside the moraines of the Lirung and Kimshung glaciers. Clear weather is most likely in October, November and April; by mid-morning clouds often rise from the lower valley.

Expect 3–4 hours up and about 2 hours down, with steady breathing at this height. The climb is a good test of how you are acclimatising: going high and sleeping low at Kyanjin is exactly what the body needs. Carry water, a warm jacket, gloves and snacks. Anyone with a worsening headache, vomiting or loss of balance should turn back and descend.

faqs.q: How hard is the Kyanjin Ri hike?
faqs.a: It is a steep but non-technical hike of about 900 m gain from Kyanjin Gompa to 4,773 m, taking 3–4 hours up and 2 hours down. The challenge is the altitude rather than the terrain. Fit first-time trekkers who have walked up the valley over three days normally manage at least the lower prayer-flag summit at about 4,600 m.

faqs.q: Kyanjin Ri or Tserko Ri, which is better?
faqs.a: Kyanjin Ri suits most trekkers: shorter, 5–6 hours return, and a strong view of Langtang Lirung. Tserko Ri at 4,984 m is a full 8–9 hour day on looser trail with a broader panorama including Yala Peak. Choose Tserko Ri only if you are fit, well acclimatised and have an extra day at Kyanjin.

faqs.q: What should I carry for Kyanjin Ri?
faqs.a: Carry 1.5–2 litres of water, a down or fleece jacket, windproof shell, gloves, warm hat, sunglasses and sunscreen, plus snacks like chocolate, nuts or yak cheese. A headlamp is needed for a pre-dawn start. Trekking poles help on the descent, which is steep and slippery with frost in the early morning.

experiences.title: Yak cheese factory and tasting at Kyanjin
experiences.price_hint: Cheese ≈ NPR 300–500 per 100 g, check locally
experiences.summary: A short visit to the cheese factory founded at Kyanjin in 1955 with Swiss help, where milk from upper-valley herders is pressed into hard cheese. Buy a slice, try it on toast at your lodge and learn how yak herding works at 3,870 m.
body: The cheese factory at Kyanjin dates from 1955, when Swiss technical assistance introduced cheese-making to give herders a way to turn surplus milk into something that keeps and sells. The building is modest, at the edge of the village near the yak pastures, and production depends on the season: it works mainly from late spring to autumn when animals graze in the upper valley and milk is plentiful.

What is made here is a firm, pale yellow cheese closer to a mountain cheese from the Alps than to the hard dried chhurpi you see in Nepali markets. Herders from the kharkas around Kyanjin and Langshisa bring milk from yaks and chauri, the yak-cow crossbreed. If the cheesemaker is around, you may see the wooden moulds and presses and the room where wheels mature.

You can buy cheese by weight at the factory or from lodges, and most kitchens in Kyanjin and Langtang village put it on toast, in pizza or in a cheese momo. A 100–200 g piece is a good snack for the Kyanjin Ri climb. If you are continuing to Gosaikunda, the smaller government dairy at Chandanbari makes cheese too, so you can compare.

faqs.q: Is the Kyanjin cheese factory still working?
faqs.a: It operates seasonally, mainly when yaks are grazing in the upper valley from late spring to autumn. Even when production pauses, cheese is usually on sale at the factory or in lodges. Opening hours are informal, so ask your lodge owner in the afternoon. Check current status before you travel if seeing it working is important to you.

Most of the milk comes from female yaks, called nak, and from chauri, a yak and cow crossbreed that gives more milk. The cheese is a hard, mild mountain cheese. Strictly, male yaks do not give milk, which is why locals smile when trekkers ask for yak milk; the female animal is the nak.

faqs.q: Can I take yak cheese back to India or abroad?
faqs.a: Hard cheese travels well in a sealed bag for a week or two at cool temperatures. For India, small personal quantities are normally fine in checked baggage. Many other countries restrict dairy imports, so check your home country's customs rules before buying a large block. Keep it out of hot cars in Kathmandu.

experiences.title: Langshisa Kharka walk to the Langtang Glacier
experiences.summary: A long but gentle day east along the upper valley floor from Kyanjin to the yak pastures of Langshisa Kharka at about 4,100 m, with moraines, glacial streams and close views of the Langtang Glacier system.
body: Beyond Kyanjin the Langtang Valley keeps going east for another 15–20 km to the Tibetan border, but few trekkers see it. The walk to Langshisa Kharka follows the north bank of the Langtang Khola across wide gravel flats and grassy kharkas used by yak herders in summer. Height gain is only about 250 m, so it is less tiring than Kyanjin Ri, though the distance is long at roughly 16 km return.

The scenery is different from the lower valley: broad glacial outwash, braided streams, stone huts and the grey moraines of the Langtang Glacier, one of the longest in the region. Langshisa Ri rises above the confluence, and on clear days you look up side valleys to peaks on the border. Bearded vultures and Himalayan griffons often circle overhead, and blue sheep are seen on the slopes.

There are no lodges past Kyanjin, so carry lunch, water and warm clothes; your lodge can pack boiled eggs, chapati and cheese. Start early because afternoon wind funnels up the valley. The walk adds an extra day to a standard itinerary and is a good alternative for those who prefer distance to steep climbs, or a second acclimatisation day before Yala Peak or Tserko Ri.

faqs.q: How far is Langshisa Kharka from Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Langshisa Kharka is about 8 km east of Kyanjin Gompa along the valley floor, at around 4,100 m. Most people take 3.5–4 hours out and 3 hours back, making a 7–8 hour day with only about 250 m of height gain. It is long rather than steep, but there are no lodges, so carry food and water.

faqs.q: Can I see the Langtang Glacier on this walk?
faqs.a: You see the lower Langtang Glacier system, its moraines and the meltwater streams that feed the Langtang Khola, plus smaller glaciers spilling off Langshisa Ri and nearby peaks. Reaching the main glacier tongue further up-valley requires camping and more days, which is outside standard teahouse treks.

faqs.q: Is a guide needed beyond Kyanjin?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign trekkers need a licensed guide anywhere in Langtang National Park under the rules in force since 2023, and beyond Kyanjin there are no lodges or people for help. The trail is easy to follow in good weather, but fog and snow can hide it. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Kyanjin Gompa sits at about 3,870 m, the highest overnight stop on the standard Langtang Valley trek. Above it, Kyanjin Ri reaches 4,773 m and Tserko Ri 4,984 m. Because of the height, we schedule two nights here with a day hike up and back, which helps acclimatisation before the descent.

faqs.q: How many days does it take to reach Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Three walking days from Syabrubesi: day one to Lama Hotel (about 6 hours), day two to Langtang village (6–7 hours) and day three to Kyanjin Gompa (3–4 hours). Add one day for the 122 km drive from Kathmandu. The return takes two walking days, so a full trek is usually 7–8 days.

faqs.q: Can I fly to Kyanjin Gompa by helicopter?
faqs.a: Yes. Helicopter tours from Kathmandu land at Kyanjin in about 40 minutes, weather permitting, usually for a short breakfast stop before flying back. Some trekkers also fly out from Kyanjin at the end of a trek. Flights run in the morning only, as clouds build in the valley by midday.

faqs.q: Is there altitude sickness risk at Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Yes, at 3,870 m mild symptoms such as headache, poor sleep and loss of appetite are common, and serious altitude sickness is possible if you ascend too fast. The standard itinerary climbs gradually over three days. Drink plenty, avoid alcohol, and descend if symptoms worsen. Consult your doctor about acetazolamide before you go.

faqs.q: What is the weather at Kyanjin Gompa in October?
faqs.a: October is one of the clearest months. Expect sunny mornings with daytime temperatures of about 8–12 °C and nights around −2 to −5 °C. Afternoon cloud and wind are common. Snow can fall at any time, so carry warm layers. By late November nights drop towards −10 °C.

faqs.q: Is there Wi-Fi and charging at Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Most lodges offer Wi-Fi and phone charging for a fee, powered by solar panels or small hydro schemes. Speeds are slow and connections drop in bad weather. Mobile data works in parts of the village. Bring a power bank because cold drains batteries quickly at night.

faqs.q: What is there to do at Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Climb Kyanjin Ri (4,773 m) or Tserko Ri (4,984 m), visit the monastery and the 1955 yak cheese factory, walk up the valley to Langshisa Kharka, or simply rest and watch Langtang Lirung change colour at sunset. Strong walkers with climbing experience can also attempt Yala Peak at 5,500 m from here.

faqs.q: Can children go to Kyanjin Gompa?
faqs.a: Fit children aged about 10 and above who have walked hills before can reach Kyanjin with a slow itinerary and an extra night at Langtang village. The main concern is altitude: young children may not report symptoms clearly, so parents must watch closely. Families with younger children often prefer the helicopter tour or lower treks.

faqs.q: Was Kyanjin Gompa damaged in the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Yes. The 2015 earthquake damaged the monastery and lodges, though Kyanjin escaped the avalanche that destroyed Langtang village further down. Lodges were rebuilt and enlarged within a few years, and the trek has fully reopened. Today the village has more and better lodges than before 2015.
